texto: Ten men went to Pearl Harbor in secret submarines. Nine died, and Japan honored them as heroes. So what happened to number ten?
Kazuo Sakamaki's compass was broken before he launched. He went anyway.
He hit a reef, again and again. A destroyer opened fire. Gas filled the hull, and he lost consciousness. His torpedoes never fired.
He ran aground in Hawaii, and lit the fuse to destroy his sub. It did not explode. His crewman drowned.
He became America's first Japanese prisoner of the war. He asked to be allowed to die. The answer was no.
So Japan struck his name from its records. The official painting shows nine faces.
America put his submarine on a truck, and toured it through forty-one states to sell war bonds.
And according to his memoir, the man who asked to die tried to talk other prisoners out of it.
He came home, joined Toyota, and stayed silent for decades.
Fifty years later, he stood in front of that submarine in Texas, reportedly in tears.
Japan's monument to that mission? It says nine.
